unit.title: Scoring and Rotation
unit.summary: Side-out and rally scoring rules, the three-number score call, server rotation, the 0-0-2 start, and why court position matters.

lessons.title: Only the server scores
lessons.objective: Explain side-out scoring and why the serving advantage matters.

payload.prompt: In side-out scoring, what happens when the receiving team wins a rally?

options.text: They gain the serve without scoring (side-out)

explanation.correct: Side-out means the receiving team wins the serve, but no one scores a point. Only the serving side can score.
explanation.incorrect: In side-out scoring, only the server scores points. The receiving team gets the serve if they win, but with zero points.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out: you win the serve but don't score until you serve.

payload.prompt: Complete the side-out rule.
payload.template: Only the {{scorer}} scores points in side-out scoring; the other team must {{action}} to start scoring.

explanation.correct: The serving team scores; the receiving team must win the serve to start accumulating points of their own.
explanation.incorrect: Side-out scoring reserves scoring for the serving team. The receiving team gains the serve (side-out) with no points.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server scores; you get the serve to start scoring.

payload.prompt: Your team is receiving. You win the rally. Do you score?

situation.narrative: It's 3-2 in side-out scoring, your team is receiving. You hit a clean winner.

options.label: You gain the serve but don't score
options.consequence: You become the serving team with the score still 3-2. Now you can start scoring points.
considerations: Side-out scoring only lets the server score
Winning the rally as receiver = side-out (gain serve)
Next point you play will be your first chance to score

options.label: You score one point
options.consequence: Incorrect. The receiving team never scores in side-out; you gain the serve to start scoring.
considerations: This is the core rule of side-out
You must serve to accumulate points
Side-out is 'serve to score'

payload.expertNote: Side-out scoring makes the serve extremely valuable. The serving team can run up a lead; the receiving team must win the serve first to score.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We won that rally but didn't score? That doesn't make sense.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Receivers don't score. You win the serve (a side-out), and points come on your serve.
That's just the rule; nobody knows why.

payload.translation: Side-out scoring means the serving side has the scoring advantage. You must win the serve before you can start scoring.

followUps.line: You got the serve (side-out). Now you score on your serves until they win.
followUps.why: Explains the rule and its effect clearly.

followUps.line: Side-out scoring: only the server scores. You won the serve, which is huge.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Side-out is the foundation of pickleball scoring strategy. Winning the serve is as important as scoring points.

payload.prompt: It's 6-5 to the servers. The receivers win the rally. Score?

scene.alt: Score scenario: the serving team leads 6-5 and the receiving team wins the rally.

explanation.correct: Receivers never score in side-out scoring. They win the serve, so the points stay 6-5 and the new serving team calls it as 5-6.
explanation.incorrect: Only the serving team can score. The receivers' reward for winning the rally is the serve, not a point.
explanation.sayThisLine: They win the serve, but the score stays 6-5.

lessons.title: The three-number call
lessons.objective: Read and call a doubles score as three numbers.

payload.prompt: What do the three numbers in '4-3-2' represent?

options.text: Server one score, server two score, receiver score
Serving team score, receiving team score, server number

explanation.correct: In doubles, the call is always serving team score, receiving team score, server number (1 or 2).
explanation.incorrect: The three numbers are: serving team, receiving team, then which server (server one or server two) is currently serving.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three numbers: server score, receiver score, server one or two.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Serving team is at 6, receiving is at 5, and server one is serving.
It's the first game, no idea what the other numbers mean.

payload.translation: Sam heard the score call in side-out doubles: the serving team's score, the receiving team's score, then which server is up.

followUps.line: The first number is the server's score, second is the receiver's, third is server one or two.
followUps.why: Breaks it down into memorable parts.

followUps.line: I think 6-5-1 means the servers lead 6 to 5 and the first server is up.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The three-number call is standard and becomes automatic once you use it a few times.

payload.prompt: Match each part of a three-number score call to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Which server is currently serving (1 or 2)

explanation.summary: In side-out doubles the call is serving team score, receiving team score, server number. The serving team's number always comes first.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server score, receiver score, server one or two.

payload.prompt: Complete the three-number rule.
payload.template: A doubles score is called {{num1}}, {{num2}}, {{num3}}, where the last number is always 1 or 2.

explanation.correct: In side-out doubles the call runs server's team, receiver's team, then server one or two.
explanation.incorrect: Always remember the order: serving team first, receiving second, server number third (1 or 2).
explanation.sayThisLine: Three numbers: server, receiver, and which server's turn.

payload.prompt: You need to call the score. What is it?

situation.narrative: You're keeping score. The serving team has 7 points, the receiving team has 4, and it's the second server's turn.

options.label: Call it 7-4-2
options.consequence: Correct. Seven (server), four (receiver), two (server two is serving). This is the proper three-number call.
considerations: 7 for the serving team
4 for the receiving team
2 because server two is up

options.label: Call it 4-7-2
options.consequence: Incorrect order. The serving team score always comes first in the three-number call.
considerations: Server score first, receiver score second
Confusing scores makes play confusing
Get the order right for clarity

payload.expertNote: Serving team first, receiving team second, server number last. The server calls it out loud before every serve, so you get plenty of practice.

lessons.title: Server one, server two, side out
lessons.objective: Follow the serve through both partners and know when the serve moves to the other team.

payload.prompt: Put one serving turn in order, from server one to side-out.

items.text: Server one wins a rally: the team scores and server one serves again
items.why: Winning a rally scores a point and keeps the serve.

items.text: Server one loses a rally: server two takes over
items.why: The first server is out, so the serve moves to the partner.

items.text: Server two wins a rally: the team scores and server two serves again
items.why: The second partner also keeps serving while they keep winning.

items.text: Server two loses a rally: both partners have had their turn
items.why: Losing as server two ends the team's time serving.

items.text: The other team takes the serve (a side-out)
items.why: The serve passes to the other team once both partners have lost a rally.

explanation.correct: Server one serves until they lose a rally, then server two does, then it is a side-out and the other team takes the serve.
explanation.incorrect: Each partner keeps serving as long as they keep winning. A lost rally moves the serve to the partner, and a second lost rally sends it to the other team.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server one, then server two, then the serve goes to the other team.

payload.prompt: Mid-game, server one loses a rally. The serve moves to...?

scene.alt: Serve scenario in the middle of a game: server one just lost the rally.

explanation.correct: Server one is out, so the serve goes to server two on the same team. Only after server two loses does it go to the other team (side-out).
explanation.incorrect: Apart from the very start of a game, each team has two servers (both partners). Server one losing means server two gets a turn; side-out happens only after both lose.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server one out, server two gets the serve.

payload.prompt: Server two just lost. The serve moves to...?

scene.alt: Serve scenario: server two just lost the rally, completing the pair's turn.

explanation.correct: Both servers on the serving team have lost; it's a side-out. The receiving team now serves.
explanation.incorrect: When both partners lose, the serve goes to the receiving team. You don't start over with server one.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out, they get the serve.

payload.prompt: Complete the server rotation rule.
payload.template: The serve goes to {{first}}, then {{second}}, then a {{third}} to the other team if both lose.

explanation.correct: Both partners on the serving team get a turn. After both lose a rally, side-out sends the serve to the other team.
explanation.incorrect: A serving team has two servers after the opening turn. Only after both have lost a rally does the other team get the serve.
explanation.sayThisLine: Server one, server two, then side-out.

payload.prompt: Server one wins the rally. Where does the serve go next?

situation.narrative: Server one just won a rally. The call is now 7-2-1, so the serving team leads.

options.label: Server one keeps serving
options.consequence: Right. When the server wins a rally the team scores and the same server serves again, from the other side. Server one keeps going until they lose a rally.
considerations: Winning the rally = you keep the serve
Server one plays until they lose
Then server two gets their chance

options.label: Serve goes to server two
options.consequence: Incorrect. You only move to the other partner after losing, not after winning.
considerations: Winning keeps you serving
Losing moves to the other server
Side-out happens after both lose

payload.expertNote: The serving team can run long scoring streaks. As long as they keep winning, the serve stays with them (server one, then server two if needed).

lessons.title: The 0-0-2 start
lessons.objective: Know why the first serving team starts with only one server.

payload.prompt: Why does the first serving team start a game at 0-0-2?

options.text: Because server two is the better player
So serving first is not a double advantage

explanation.correct: Only the serving team can score, so serving first is an edge. Starting at 0-0-2 means the first server counts as server two, so their team has no second server: their first lost rally is an immediate side-out.
explanation.incorrect: The 2 is not about skill, chance or speed. It cuts the first serving team down to one turn, which evens out the advantage of serving first.
explanation.sayThisLine: The first team gets one turn at the start, so serving first isn't too big an edge.

payload.prompt: The game starts at 0-0-2 and the server wins the rally. What next?

situation.narrative: The game has just started at 0-0-2. The first serving team wins the rally.

facts.label: Start of game
facts.value: 0-0-2, the only server on their team

options.label: The same server serves again, from the other side
options.consequence: Right. Winning a rally scores a point and keeps the serve. The starting server keeps going until they lose a rally.
considerations: Winning keeps you serving
0-0-2 only limits the team to one turn
The turn ends on their first lost rally

options.label: The other team gets the serve right away
options.consequence: Not yet. The serve only changes hands when the serving team loses a rally. At 0-0-2 that comes straight after the first loss, not after a win.
considerations: The starting server has no partner turn
But winning a rally does not end their turn
Side-out happens when they lose a rally

payload.expertNote: 0-0-2 only affects the opening turn: the first server has no partner behind them. As long as they keep winning rallies, they keep serving.

payload.prompt: Complete the 0-0-2 rule.
payload.template: A game starts 0-0-{{num}}, so the first serving team gets only {{turns}} turn before a side-out.

explanation.correct: The call is 0-0-2: no points yet, and the starting server counts as server two. With no second server behind them, the team's first lost rally sends the serve to the other team.
explanation.incorrect: The starting server counts as server two, not server one. That leaves no partner turn, so the serve changes hands after the first lost rally.
explanation.sayThisLine: We start at 0-0-2, so our first lost rally is a side-out.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Why does the first team only get one server at 0-0-2?

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Serving is an advantage in side-out, so the first team gets only one server to make it fair.
I don't know, that's just the rule.
It's a penalty for being first.
So the other team can catch up faster.

payload.translation: Only the serving team can score, so serving first is a real edge. Starting at 0-0-2 gives that team just one turn, which evens things out.

followUps.line: I think it's because only the serving team scores, so serving first would be too big an edge.
followUps.why: Gives the reason in your own words and is honest about how sure you are.

followUps.line: After that first turn, the other team gets the serve. That keeps the start fair.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The 0-0-2 rule is a fairness adjustment, not a penalty. If Sam wants more detail, asking who taught them the rule is a fine follow-up.

payload.prompt: Game start, 0-0-2. The server loses the first rally. What now?

scene.alt: Start of a game: the first serving team is at 0-0-2 and their server just lost the rally.

explanation.correct: The starting server counts as server two, so there is no partner turn left. One lost rally at 0-0-2 is an immediate side-out.
explanation.incorrect: The partner does not get a turn at the start of a game. Because the call is 0-0-2, the serve goes to the other team after the first lost rally.
explanation.sayThisLine: At 0-0-2, one lost rally and the other team serves.

lessons.title: Even right, odd left
lessons.objective: Pick the service side based on the serving team's score.

payload.prompt: Score is 5-3-1. Server one is serving. Which side?

diagram.alt: Top-down pickleball court. You are the server, standing behind the near baseline and facing the net, with a left and a right service side.

hotspots.label: Left box, as the server sees it
Right box, as the server sees it

explanation.correct: The serving team has 5, which is odd, so server one serves from the left side. Odd means left.
explanation.incorrect: When the serving team's score is odd (like 5), the server stands on the left. When it is even (0, 2, 4, 6), the server stands on the right.
explanation.sayThisLine: Odd score means left side, even means right.

payload.prompt: Score is 6-4-2. Which side does server two serve from?

explanation.correct: The serving team has 6, which is even, so the server stands on the right. Even means right, whether it is server one or server two.
explanation.incorrect: The side comes from the serving team's score, not the server number. Six is even, so right. Left is for odd scores.
explanation.sayThisLine: Even score means right side; odd means left.

payload.prompt: Score is 3-2-1. Where does server one start?

explanation.correct: The serving team has 3, which is odd, so the server stands on the left. Odd means left; even means right.
explanation.incorrect: For serving position, use the serving team's score, the first number. Three is odd, which means the left side.
explanation.sayThisLine: Odd score means left side; even means right.

payload.prompt: Complete the serving position rule.
payload.template: If the serving team's score is {{even}}, the server stands on the right; if {{odd}}, on the left.

explanation.correct: Even score = right side. Odd score = left side. This applies every single serve.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is consistent: even right, odd left. It determines which service box the server serves from on each rally.
explanation.sayThisLine: Even right, odd left. That's how you know where to stand.

payload.prompt: Score is 2-1-1. Where does server one serve from?

situation.narrative: The serving team has 2 points and server one is up. Which side of the baseline does the server stand on?

options.label: Right side (the server's right)
options.consequence: Right. Two is even, so the server stands on the right and serves into the diagonal box from there.
considerations: 2 points is even
Even score means the right side
The server stands behind the right half of the baseline

options.label: Left side (the server's left)
options.consequence: Not quite. Two is even, not odd, so the server starts on the right.
considerations: Left side is for odd scores (1, 3, 5, etc.)
2 is even, so right side
Remember: even right, odd left

payload.expertNote: The even-odd rule feels automatic after a few games. It keeps everyone standing where the score says they should, so there is always a way to check.

payload.prompt: Tied 10-10. What's the lowest score the winner can finish on?

explanation.correct: From 10-10, 11-10 is not enough because a game has to be won by two. The earliest finish is 12-10.
explanation.incorrect: You need 11 points and a two-point lead. From a tie at 10, the quickest way is 12-10.
explanation.sayThisLine: You need 11, and you have to win by two.

payload.prompt: What's the minimum winning score in a standard pickleball game?

explanation.correct: A standard game is to 11, win by two. So 11-9 ends it, but at 11-10 play goes on until someone leads by two.
explanation.incorrect: The usual target in side-out play is 11, not 15 or 21, and a game must be won by two. Some events and formats use other targets.
explanation.sayThisLine: Games go to 11, and you win by two.

payload.prompt: What's the common match format in tournament pickleball?

explanation.correct: Best of three is the common format: the first team to win two games wins the match. Some events play a single game, so check the format.
explanation.incorrect: Tournament matches are usually best of three games, not sets. Rec play is often just one game at a time.
explanation.sayThisLine: Matches are usually best of three games.

payload.prompt: Complete the game and match rules.
payload.template: A game is played to {{goal}} and won by {{margin}}; a match is {{format}} games.

explanation.correct: Side-out games go to 11, win by 2. A match is usually best of three, so the first team to win two games takes it.
explanation.incorrect: The usual setup is a game to 11, won by two, with matches best of three. Events can differ, so check the format.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eleven, win by two; matches are usually best of three.

payload.prompt: Up a game, and 10-9 in game two. What's at stake?

situation.narrative: It's a best-of-three match and your team won game one 11-8. Game two is close, and you are serving at 10-9.

facts.label: To win the match
facts.value: First team to win two games

options.label: Win the next rally and you win the game and the match
options.consequence: Right. At 10-9 one more point makes it 11-9, which wins game two. With game one already yours, that wins the match.
considerations: 11-9 is a two-point lead, so the game ends
Two game wins take the match
You are serving, so you can score

options.label: Win the next rally and it goes to a third game
options.consequence: Not quite. You already won game one, so winning game two makes it 2-0 and the match is over.
considerations: You already have one game win
A third game only happens at 1-1
One more rally win ends it here

payload.expertNote: At 10-9, losing the next rally hands the serve to the other team, who can tie it at 10-10. That is why these points feel so big.

lessons.title: Rally scoring
lessons.objective: Explain rally scoring and where it is used.

payload.prompt: In rally scoring, what happens every rally?

options.text: Only the server scores if they win
Whoever wins the rally scores a point
No one scores until a team reaches 5

explanation.correct: In rally scoring every rally is worth a point, and the rally winner gets it whether or not they were serving.
explanation.incorrect: Only the server scoring is side-out scoring, the traditional way. Rally scoring gives the point to the rally winner every time.
explanation.sayThisLine: In rally scoring, every rally gives somebody a point.

payload.prompt: Match the scoring types to their rule.

pairs.definition: Only the serving team scores points; receiving team must win the serve first.
Every rally awards a point to the winner, regardless of who is serving.
In side-out scoring, the server has an edge because they accumulate points while serving.

distractorDefinitions: A bonus point for winning a long rally
Points only count on the second serve of a turn

explanation.summary: Side-out is the traditional way. Rally scoring is an allowed option in the current rulebook, though some events still require side-out.
explanation.sayThisLine: Side-out: server only. Rally: everybody scores on every rally.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We played rally scoring tonight. It's so different.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Yeah, every rally somebody scores. Do you prefer it over side-out?
I don't know what that means.

payload.translation: Sam played with rally scoring, where every rally gives the winner a point. It changes how the game feels compared with side-out.

followUps.line: I've heard some pro events use rally scoring at times. Did it change how you played?
followUps.why: Shows some context and invites Sam's take, without pretending to know more.

followUps.line: Every rally counts instead of just the server's. Did that speed things up?
followUps.why: A curious question about the effect.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Rally scoring is debated, and plenty of players love it while others prefer side-out. Listen to Sam's take instead of picking a side.

payload.prompt: Complete the rally scoring rule.
payload.template: In rally scoring, the team that wins the rally {{result}}. In side-out scoring, only the {{who}} can score.

explanation.correct: Rally scoring gives the point to whoever wins the rally. Side-out scoring only lets the serving team score.
explanation.incorrect: The difference is who can score. Rally scoring: the rally winner, every time. Side-out: only the serving team. Target scores depend on the event, so check the format.
explanation.sayThisLine: In rally scoring, every rally counts.

payload.prompt: You're receiving and you win the rally. Under rally scoring, do you score?

situation.narrative: Rally scoring is in effect. You're on the receiving team and you win the rally.

options.label: Yes, you score a point
options.consequence: Right. In rally scoring the rally winner scores, no matter who is serving. You won the rally, so you score.
considerations: Rally scoring = every rally counts
You don't have to serve to score
Different from side-out

options.label: No, you only gain the serve
options.consequence: Incorrect. That's side-out scoring. Rally scoring gives you a point for winning the rally.
considerations: Rally scoring means everybody can score
You don't need to serve to score
This is the key difference from side-out

payload.expertNote: Rally scoring takes away the serving edge, because every rally counts. It is an option in the current rulebook and some events use it.

lessons.title: Keep the score, keep the peace
lessons.objective: Track a full game and settle a score dispute.

payload.prompt: Both teams remember a different score. How do you settle it?

situation.narrative: Mid-game, the two teams disagree. One says the last call was 7-5-1, the other swears it was 6-5-1.

options.label: Pause, talk it through calmly, and agree on the last point everyone remembers
options.consequence: Good. Retracing the last few rallies together usually settles it, and you can carry on from there. It keeps the game friendly.
considerations: Talk through the last few rallies together
Agree on the last point everyone remembers
A friendly game matters more than the exact point

options.label: Make them prove it, and accuse them of cheating if they can't
options.consequence: That escalates it. Memories slip for everyone, and an accusation can end a game and a friendship.
considerations: Most disputes are honest memory slips
Accusations turn a mix-up into a fight
Calm talk solves it faster

payload.expertNote: Disputes usually come from honest memory slips. The best fix is prevention: the server calls the score out loud before every serve, so everyone hears it.

payload.prompt: Score is 8-5-1. Server one wins the rally. What's the new call?

scene.alt: Score scenario: the serving team leads 8-5 with server one serving, and server one wins the rally.

explanation.correct: The serving team scores, so 8 becomes 9. Server one keeps serving after a win, so the server number stays 1.
explanation.incorrect: The server number only changes when the server loses a rally. After a win, the same server keeps serving, so it stays 1.
explanation.sayThisLine: A win adds a point, and the same server keeps serving.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: Wait, what's the score? I lost track after all those fast rallies.

payload.question: What should you say?

options.text: Easy to lose track! The server calls it before each serve: their score, ours, then 1 or 2.
I don't remember either, let's just restart.

payload.translation: Losing track is normal. The server is supposed to call the score out loud before every serve, so Sam can just listen for the next call.

followUps.line: Totally happens. Let's listen for the next call: server's score, receiver's score, then 1 or 2.
followUps.why: Reassures Sam and points to the real fix.

followUps.line: If we all say it out loud each time, nobody has to remember it.
followUps.why: A friendly suggestion for the group.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know the exact score to help. Pointing Sam to the next call keeps things easy, and it is fine to say you lost track too.

payload.title: Sorting out the score

exchanges.theirMessage: Is it 5-3 or 3-5? I can't remember who's serving.

replies.text: The serving team's score is always said first. Who's serving right now?
replies.theirResponse: We are. So it's 5-3. Got it, thanks.
replies.coachNote: You used the rule to help Sam work it out instead of guessing.

replies.text: I think 5-3, but I'm not sure who's up.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, so we have to remember that too.
replies.coachNote: Honest, but the serving team's number always comes first, so who is serving settles it.

replies.text: Honestly, does it matter? Let's just keep playing.
replies.theirResponse: Um, it does. I want to know where we are.
replies.coachNote: Knowing the score matters to Sam. Take a breath and help work it out.

exchanges.theirMessage: Okay, and after I serve, is it still server one or does it become server two?

replies.text: I think it depends. Win the rally and you keep serving as server one. Lose it and your partner becomes server two.
replies.theirResponse: Oh! So the server number only changes if I lose.
replies.coachNote: You shared what you know and were honest about how sure you are.

replies.text: It goes to server two next.
replies.coachNote: Winning keeps the serve with you, so the number stays the same.

replies.text: It always changes after one serve. Everyone knows that.
replies.theirResponse: Hm, I don't think that's right...
replies.coachNote: Confident but wrong. Saying 'I think winners keep serving, let's check' works better.

payload.closingNote: Keeping score is a shared job. The server calls it out loud before every serve, and a friendly chat settles most disputes.
